variants.name: ExecutorService + Callable/Future over a fixed thread pool (Java 5)
variants.implementation_notes: Java's classic realization is java.util.concurrent: the master creates a bounded pool (Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) or newWorkStealingPool) and submits Callable sub-tasks; invokeAll() is the bulk dispatch that waits until every task is done and returns Futures in input order, while submit() plus Future.get() joins individually. Future.get() rethrows a failed task's exception wrapped in ExecutionException, cancel(true) is cooperative (it only interrupts), and the documented memory rule is that actions before submission happen-before the task, which happens-before retrieving the result via Future.get(). Lifecycle is shutdown()/shutdownNow() plus awaitTermination(), or try-with-resources on Java 19+ where ExecutorService is AutoCloseable. Because the classic structure is the API here, prefer it over hand-rolled worker loops.
pitfalls: A pool sized to the cores with blocking sub-tasks serialises or deadlocks: size it for the workload and give Future.get() a timeout instead of waiting forever on a lost worker.
invokeAll(..., timeout, unit) cancels only the unfinished futures - the underlying tasks keep running unless they respond to interruption.
Exceptions inside tasks stay invisible until a join observes them; nothing in the pool reports a failed sub-task that nobody waits on.
State shared by Callables races: only submission and result retrieval have happens-before edges.

variants.name: CompletableFuture dispatch with allOf and continuation composition (Java 8)
variants.implementation_notes: CompletableFuture turns dispatch and combination into a declarative pipeline: supplyAsync(..., executor) starts each sub-task, allOf(...) is the join that completes when every stage is done, thenApply/streams of join() combine the partials, and exceptionally/handle attach the failure policy to the stage instead of waiting and catching. The trap is the executor default - the *Async methods without an explicit Executor run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which is shared with parallel streams and must not host blocking work - so pass the master's own executor for anything that blocks or is long-running. allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void>, so the partials must be collected from the stage list, and cancellation does not propagate: complete exceptionally or cancel stages explicitly.
variants.code_sketch:
var pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers);
List<CompletableFuture<Double>> parts = IntStream.range(0, workers)
    .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> computePart(i), pool))
    .toList();                                                  // dispatch
CompletableFuture.allOf(parts.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); // join
double total = parts.stream().mapToDouble(CompletableFuture::join).sum();  // combine
pitfalls: Omitting the executor in *Async methods puts the sub-tasks on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(): blocking work there starves every parallel stream in the JVM.
allOf's Void result hides the partials and its exceptional completion reports only that some stage failed; inspect each stage or collect with a joinable list.
Cancelling the composed future does not cancel the running stages, and a stage nobody joined swallows its exception until it is read.

variants.name: One virtual thread per sub-task on Java 21+
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 21+ the master can afford a thread per sub-task: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor creates a virtual thread for each submitted task and close() (implicit in try-with-resources) waits for them all, which keeps blocking sub-tasks cheap and preserves ordinary sequential composition instead of callback chains. JEP 444 is explicit that virtual threads are cheap and must never be pooled - limiting concurrency is a job for semaphores or a dedicated pool, not a virtual-thread pool - and that blocking while pinned (inside synchronized or a native frame) captures the carrier, so hot synchronized blocks guarding I/O should move to ReentrantLock. Virtual threads add throughput, not speed: CPU-bound work still belongs on a fixed platform-thread pool.
pitfalls: Pooling virtual threads reintroduces the constraint they remove - and thread-locals or per-task caches become expensive at millions of tasks.
Pinning: a virtual thread blocking inside synchronized or a native frame captures its carrier; use ReentrantLock around blocking sections on the versions where pinning still occurs.
No speedup for CPU-bound sub-tasks: a million virtual threads on eight cores still run eight at a time, so fixed pools remain the CPU answer.
